SECTION: Automation in Everyday Life - Automation in Everyday Life (Pages 2-11)

TOPICS: public opinion on automation, survey methodology, attitudes toward specific technologies, workforce impacts, policy preferences, demographic differences, future expectations

TEXT_EVIDENCE:
- Pew Research Center is a nonpartisan fact tank that conducts public opinion polling, demographic research, content analysis, and other data-driven social science research (Page 2)
- The Center's focus areas include U.S. politics and policy; journalism and media; internet, science and technology; religion and public life; Hispanic trends; global attitudes and trends; and U.S. social and demographic trends (Page 2)
- All reports are available at www.pewresearch.org (Page 2)
- Pew Research Center is a subsidiary of The Pew Charitable Trusts, its primary funder (Page 2)
- A Pew Research Center survey of 4,135 U.S. adults was conducted May 1-15, 2017 (Page 3)
- Americans express more worry than enthusiasm about coming developments in automation (Page 3)
- The survey presented four scenarios: autonomous vehicles, robots performing human jobs, robot caregivers, and automated job candidate selection (Page 3)
- Some scenarios are more realistic than others; for example, computer algorithms are already used in hiring, but fully autonomous vehicles are not yet available (Page 3)
- Americans are roughly twice as likely to express worry (72%) than enthusiasm (33%) about robots and computers doing many human jobs (Page 4)
- They are around three times as likely to express worry (67%) than enthusiasm (22%) about algorithms making hiring decisions without human involvement (Page 4)
- 76% of Americans expect economic inequality will become much worse if robots perform many human jobs (Page 4)
- 75% anticipate the economy will not create many new, better-paying jobs for humans (Page 4)
- 64% expect people will have a hard time finding things to do with their lives if competing with advanced robots (Page 4)
- 75% anticipate driverless vehicles will help the elderly and disabled live more independently (Page 4)
- 81% expect many people who drive for a living will suffer job losses (Page 4)
- A plurality (39%) expects the number of traffic accident deaths/injuries will decrease (Page 4)
- 30% of Americans think autonomous vehicles will make roads less safe (Page 5)
- 70% anticipate robot caregivers would help alleviate the burden of caring for aging relatives (Page 5)
- 64% expect robot caregivers would increase feelings of isolation (Page 5)
- Nearly six-in-ten (56%) Americans say they would not want to ride in a driverless vehicle (Page 5)
- 59% would not want to use a robot caregiver (Page 5)
- 76% would not want to apply for a job that used a computer program to evaluate and select applicants (Page 5)
- The primary reasons for hesitation are a lack of trust, fear of losing control, and safety concerns (Page 5)
- The public generally supports policies that limit automation or bring humans more fully into the process (Page 5)
- 85% of Americans support limiting machines to dangerous or unhealthy jobs (Page 6)
- 60% support a guaranteed income for all Americans (Page 6)
- 58% support a national service program paying people for jobs machines could do faster/cheaper (Page 6)
- 58% believe there should be limits on job replacement by machines, while 41% disagree (Page 6)
- Democrats are substantially more likely than Republicans to support universal income (77% vs 38%) and national service (66% vs 46%) (Page 6)
- 60% of Democrats and 54% of Republicans support limits on job replacement (Page 6)
- 87% of Americans favor requiring a human in the driver's seat for emergency control, with 53% strongly favoring it (Page 7)
- 48% of Americans would feel better about robot caregivers if monitored by a human operator (Page 7)
- 57% would feel better about hiring algorithms if used only for initial screening before interviews (Page 7)
- A key attitudinal divide exists between technology enthusiasts and the hesitant, with enthusiasts expressing substantially more positive attitudes and anticipating wider societal benefits (Page 7)
- 77% of U.S. adults believe robots and computers could eventually perform many human jobs (Page 8)
- 20% describe this prospect as extremely realistic (Page 8)
- 30% of currently employed workers think it's at least somewhat likely their own job will be automated (Page 8)
- Americans expect significant changes to the nature of work due to automation in the coming decades (Page 8)
- Driverless vehicle users express greater enthusiasm and less worry about the technology compared to those who are more reticent (Page 8)
- 6% of U.S. adults report being impacted by automation (2% lost jobs, 5% had pay/hours reduced) (Page 9)
- 11% of 18-24 year-olds report losing a job due to automation (Page 9)
- 46% of impacted workers feel technology has decreased their career advancement opportunities (Page 9)
- 34% of impacted workers feel technology has made their work less interesting (Page 9)
- 57% of impacted workers anticipate their jobs will be mostly done by machines within their lifetimes (Page 9)
- Workers lacking a college education are much less likely to express positive attitudes towards current workforce technologies (Page 10)
- The survey asked about the impact of six common technologies: word processing/spreadsheet software, smartphones, email/social media, scheduling software, self-service customer tech, and industrial robots (Page 10)
- 24% of workers with high school diplomas or less say not a single one of the six technologies has had a positive impact on their jobs or careers (Page 10)
- For college graduates, that share is just 2% (Page 10)
- 38% of workers with high school diplomas or less indicate that technology has made their jobs more interesting (Page 10)
- 32% of workers with high school diplomas or less feel that technology has increased their opportunities for career advancement (Page 10)
- 94% of U.S. adults have some awareness of driverless vehicles (Page 11)
- 9% of U.S. adults predict most vehicles will be driverless in the next 10 years (Page 11)
- 56% expect most vehicles to be driverless in 10 to less than 50 years (Page 11)
- 79% of Americans think computer programs will diagnose and treat most diseases within 20 years (Page 11)
- 65% expect most retail interactions and city deliveries to be fully automated (Page 11)

A Pew Research Center survey of 4,135 U.S. adults conducted May 1-15, 2017, finds that many Americans anticipate significant impacts from various automation technologies in the course of their lifetimes – from the widespread adoption of autonomous vehicles to the replacement of entire job categories with robot workers. Although they expect certain positive outcomes from these developments, their attitudes more frequently reflect worry and concern over the implications of these technologies for society as a whole. To gauge the opinions of everyday Americans on this complex and far-reaching topic, the survey presented respondents with four different scenarios relating to automation technologies. Collectively, these scenarios speak to many of the hopes and concerns embedded in the broader debate over automation and its impact on society. The scenarios included: the development of autonomous vehicles that can operate without the aid of a human driver; a future in which robots and computers can perform many of the jobs currently done by human workers; the possibility of fully autonomous robot caregivers for older adults; and the possibility that a computer program could evaluate and select job candidates with no human involvement. The following are among the major findings. How realistic are the scenarios presented in the survey? Some of the scenarios presented in the survey are more futuristic than others: Today companies can utilize computer algorithms in various aspects of the hiring process - from identifying candidates who might be overlooked in traditional face-to-face recruiting, to automatically eliminating applicants who lack certain characteristics. Americans today cannot purchase a fully autonomous vehicle. But a number of companies are developing and testing these vehicles, and many modern cars offer semi-autonomous features such as adaptive cruise control or lane-assist technology. A wide range of robotic devices are being developed to help meet the demands of an aging population. But it will likely be many years before fully autonomous robot caregivers as described in this survey are available for use. More broadly, these developments speak to the possibility of a world in which robots and computer applications are capable of performing many of the tasks currently done by humans - with potentially profound implications for society as a whole.

Much of this survey focuses on possible future impacts of automation, but a minority of Americans are already being impacted by these technologies in their own jobs and careers. Specifically,  $2\%$  of Americans report that they have ever personally lost a job because their employers replaced their positions with a machine or computer program. Another  $5\%$  report that they have ever had their pay or hours reduced for the same reason. pages.ocr_text: 1. Americans' current experiences with automation and other workforce technologies The bulk of this report is focused on the coming wave of workforce automation and other automation technologies. But a variety of technological innovations – from industrial robots in manufacturing to the office productivity tools that have transformed the nature of white collar office work – have already had a profound impact on the nature of work in the present day. When asked about the impact of these and other technologies on their own jobs and careers, today's workers express decidedly mixed views. Many view these technologies in a positive light, but substantial shares view them as damaging (or at best neutral) to their own career prospects. Moreover, the survey finds that the benefits of these tools are most likely to accrue to workers with high levels of formal educational attainment. It also finds that workforce automation has already impacted a minority of today's workers in the form of lost jobs or wages – and that many of these workers view technology as a broadly negative influence on the trajectory of their own careers. elements.text: 1. Americans' current experiences with automation and other workforce technologies

The bulk of this report is focused on the coming wave of workforce automation and other automation technologies. But a variety of technological innovations – from industrial robots in manufacturing to the office productivity tools that have transformed the nature of white collar office work – have already had a profound impact on the nature of work in the present day. When asked about the impact of these and other technologies on their own jobs and careers, today's workers express decidedly mixed views. Many view these technologies in a positive light, but substantial shares view them as damaging (or at best neutral) to their own career prospects. Moreover, the survey finds that the benefits of these tools are most likely to accrue to workers with high levels of formal educational attainment. It also finds that workforce automation has already impacted a minority of today's workers in the form of lost jobs or wages – and that many of these workers view technology as a broadly negative influence on the trajectory of their own careers.

Americans' attitudes toward a future in which robots and computers can do many human jobs Discussions of the current generation of workforce automation technologies often focus on their impact on manufacturing employment and productivity. But the coming wave of advances in automation offers the potential for even greater disruption of traditional modes of work. Developments in sensors and robotics may potentially reduce the need for humans in a variety of physical applications – from taxi and truck drivers to retail store employees. Simultaneously, multipurpose artificial intelligence and machine learning technology may dramatically alter or make redundant a wide range of white collar jobs. A number of researchers have attempted to quantify the extent to which these new advancements might impact the future of work. On the other hand, others have argued that the risk these technologies pose to human employment is overblown and that they will not impact jobs in large numbers for many years, if ever. The Pew Research Center survey seeks to add to this existing body of research by gauging Americans' expectations and attitudes toward a world in which advanced robots and computer applications are competitive with human workers on a widespread scale. Specifically, respondents were asked to consider and answer questions about a scenario (highlighted in the accompanying sidebar) in which robots and computers have moved beyond performing repeated or routine tasks and are now capable of performing most of the jobs that are currently done by humans.

elements.text: For the most part, Americans consider this scenario to be plausible; express more worry than enthusiasm about the prospect of machines performing many human jobs; and anticipate more negative than positive outcomes from this development. They strongly favor the notion that machines might be limited to jobs that are dangerous or unhealthy for humans, and they offer somewhat more measured support for other types of interventions to limit the impact of widespread automation, such as the enactment of a universal basic income or national service program for displaced workers. And although they view certain jobs as being more at risk than others, a significant majority of today's workers express little concern that their own jobs or careers might be performed by machines in their lifetimes.
Broad awareness, more worry than enthusiasm about a world in which machines can perform many jobs currently done by humans

A majority of Americans are broadly familiar with the notion that automation may impact a wide range of human employment, and most consider the concept to be generally realistic. pages.ocr_text: Attitudes towards the government's obligation to take care of workers who are displaced by automation vary strongly by partisan affiliation. Some  $65\%$  of Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents feel that the government would have an obligation to take care of workers who are displaced by automation, even if that means higher taxes for others. Meanwhile, a nearly identical share of Republicans and Republican-leaning independents  $(68\%)$  feel that individuals should be responsible for their own financial well-beings even if jobs are automated on a wide scale. But despite these pronounced differences toward this aspect of the workforce automation debate, partisan opinions are much more aligned on the question of whether or not businesses should be limited in the number of human jobs they can replace with machines. TEXT_EVIDENCE:
- 79% of U.S. adults believe doctors will use computer programs to diagnose and treat most diseases within 20 years (Page 29)
- 65% expect most stores and deliveries in major cities to be fully automated (Page 29)

- Larger shares of this group believe the economy will become more efficient (55% vs. 42%) or that many new, well-paying jobs will result (37% vs. 24%) (Page 29)
- 94% of U.S. adults have heard something about the development of autonomous vehicles (Page 30)
- 35% of U.S. adults have heard "a lot" about the effort to develop driverless vehicles (Page 30)
- 66% of those who have heard at least a little about the issue have a "mix of both" positive and negative views (Page 30)
- 44% of men have heard a lot about it compared to 26% of women (Page 30)
- 43% of college graduates have heard a lot about it compared to 25% of those with a high school diploma or less (Page 30)
- 66% of those familiar with the issue have been exposed to a mix of positive and negative coverage (Page 31)
- 22% have heard mostly positive things, and 12% have heard mostly negative things (Page 31)
- 40% of U.S. adults are at least somewhat enthusiastic, while 54% express some level of worry (Page 31)
- 11% are very enthusiastic, and 14% are very worried (Page 31)
- 22% are not at all enthusiastic, compared to 11% who are not at all worried (Page 31)
- 46% of men are at least somewhat enthusiastic, compared to 34% of women (Page 31)
- 63% of women express some level of worry, compared to 44% of men (Page 31)
- 49% of college graduates and 47% of those ages 18-49 are enthusiastic (Page 31)
- 56% of Americans anticipate most vehicles will be autonomous in the next 10 to 49 years (Page 32)
- 9% expect this to happen in fewer than 10 years (Page 32)
- 8% believe it will never occur (Page 32)
- 56% of Americans would not want to ride in a driverless vehicle if given the opportunity (Page 32)
- 44% say they would ride in a driverless vehicle if given the chance (Page 32)
- Interest in riding an autonomous vehicle is higher among men (53%) than women (35%), those under 50 (51%), college graduates (56%), and urban residents (52%) (Page 33)
- 57% of those who have heard a lot about driverless vehicles would ride in one, compared to 38% who have heard a little and 23% who have heard nothing (Page 33)
- 42% of non-users cite a lack of trust or unwillingness to cede control; 30% cite safety concerns (Page 33)
- A slight majority of Americans (56%) would not want to ride in a driverless vehicle (Page 34)
- The largest reason for not wanting to ride is "Don't trust it/worried about giving up control" at 42% (Page 34)
- The largest reason for wanting to ride is "Just for the experience/think it would be cool" at 37% (Page 34)
- 17% of the surveyed group would like to ride in a driverless car because they feel these vehicles will be safer than those driven by humans (Page 35)
- 39% of U.S. adults expect traffic fatalities to decrease if driverless vehicles become widespread (Page 36)
- 30% expect fatalities to increase, and 31% expect them to stay the same (Page 36)

- The survey compares U.S. adults who would ride in a driverless vehicle versus those who would not (Page 39)
- Enthusiasts expect greater benefits (e.g., independence for elderly/disabled) and feel safer sharing the road (Page 39)

- The jobs are difficult to fill due to heavy physical demands, low wages, and benefits (Page 40)
- Most Americans have heard little about efforts to develop caregiver robots (Page 40)
- A majority of Americans find the concept of a robot caregiver realistic (Page 40)
- Respondents anticipate both positive impacts (reducing worry for young people, helping older adults be more independent) and negative impacts (older adults feeling more isolated) (Page 40)
- 65% of U.S. adults have heard nothing at all about robot caregivers for older adults (Page 41)
- Only 6% have heard a lot about this topic (Page 41)
- 59% of U.S. adults think the concept of robot caregivers seems realistic (Page 41)
- 10% describe the concept as extremely realistic (Page 41)
- 44% of Americans are at least somewhat enthusiastic about robot caregivers (Page 41)
- 47% express some level of worry about robot caregivers (Page 41)
- 38% of adults ages 50 and up are enthusiastic, compared to 49% of 18- to 49-year-olds (Page 41)
- 41% of U.S. adults would be interested in having a robot caregiver, while 59% would not (Page 42)
- Interest is higher among men (48%) than women (34%) (Page 42)
- Interest is higher among whites (43%) and Hispanics (45%) than blacks (27%) (Page 42)
- Interest is higher among college graduates (51%) than those with some college (45%) or a high school diploma or less (29%) (Page 42)
- Among those who have heard a lot about robot caregivers, 70% are interested; this drops to 48% for those who have heard only a little and 35% for those who have heard nothing (Page 42)
- 41% of U.S. adults would be interested in a robot caregiver (Page 43)
- 21% of those interested cite "would provide better quality of care" as a main reason (Page 43)
- 59% of U.S. adults would not be interested in a robot caregiver (Page 43)
- 54% of those who say no cite "No human touch or interaction" as the main reason (Page 43)
- 21% of those open to the idea of robot caregivers find it appealing because it would reduce the heavy burden placed on family members and loved ones (Page 44)
- 15% of respondents believe such robots would help older adults remain independent and in their homes longer (Page 45)
- 8% value the robot's availability during emergencies (Page 45)
- 5% each see cost savings or increased safety/security (Page 45)
- 54% of non-interest groups cite loss of human touch/compassion as the main reason against robot caregivers (Page 45)
- 12% of respondents are concerned robots might make a mistake in caring for loved ones (Page 46)
- 6% argue that caregiving is a job for family and loved ones and should not be outsourced to a machine (Page 46)
- 70% of U.S. adults think robot caregivers would allow younger people to feel less worried about taking care of aging relatives (Page 47)
- 59% of U.S. adults think robot caregivers would make older adults feel more independent and self-sufficient (Page 47)
- 64% of Americans think robot caregivers would cause the elderly to feel more isolated (Page 47)
- 42% think robot caregivers would only be used by people who could not afford a human caregiver (Page 47)
- 56% think it likely that many older adults would treat their robot caregivers like a human friend (Page 47)
- 48% of Americans would feel better about robot caregivers if a human monitored them via camera (Page 48)
- 20% would feel worse, and 32% would be unaffected by this feature (Page 48)
- 55% of adults aged 65 and older would feel better, compared to 42% of those aged 18-29 (Page 48)
- 65% of people interested in using robot caregivers say human monitoring would make them feel better, versus 36% of those not interested (Page 48)
- 83% of those interested in using robot caregivers are very or somewhat enthusiastic about the concept (Page 48)
- Just 17% of those who would not be interested in this technology share a negative view of its development (Page 49)

It highlights both positive and negative anticipated outcomes, with a bar chart showing that 70% of U.S. adults believe robot caregivers would help young people worry less about caring for aging relatives, while 64% fear they would lead to more isolation for older adults. The text also notes that 59% think robots would make older adults feel more independent, and 56% believe many older adults would treat their robot caregivers like human friends. The data is sourced from a survey conducted in May 2017.

**Text Evidence:**
- 70% of U.S. adults think robot caregivers would allow younger people to feel less worried about taking care of aging relatives.
- 59% of U.S. adults think robot caregivers would make older adults feel more independent and self-sufficient.
- 64% of Americans think robot caregivers would cause the elderly to feel more isolated.
- 42% think robot caregivers would only be used by people who could not afford a human caregiver.
- 56% think it likely that many older adults would treat their robot caregivers like a human friend.
- The survey was conducted from May 1-15, 2017.

TEXT_EVIDENCE:
- Only 17% of individuals who are not interested in robot caregivers hold a negative view of their societal development (Page 49)
- The survey examines Americans' attitudes toward hiring algorithms using a scenario described in a sidebar where computer programs score job applicants based on resumes, applications, or standardized tests to rank and hire them (Page 50)
- Few Americans have heard of or considered this specific scenario before (Page 50)
- Respondents express far more worry than enthusiasm about machines making hiring decisions (Page 50)
- A larger share expresses concern that many important qualities would be overlooked in the process (Page 50)
- Some feel the program would be less biased and make better decisions than humans (Page 50)
- 57% of Americans have heard nothing at all about computer programs reviewing job applications without human involvement (Page 51)
- Only 9% have heard a lot about this concept (Page 51)
- 59% of Americans find the concept at least somewhat realistic, while 12% find it extremely so (Page 51)
- 28% think it is not very realistic and 13% think it is not at all realistic (Page 51)
- Among those who have heard a lot about the concept, 87% find it at least somewhat realistic and 45% find it extremely realistic (Page 51)
- Just 3% of Americans are very enthusiastic about hiring algorithms, while 28% are not at all enthusiastic (Page 51)
- 21% express high levels of worry, and only 7% are not worried at all (Page 51)
- The survey was conducted from May 1-15, 2017, as part of the "Automation in Everyday Life" study (Page 51)
- 76% of U.S. adults would not want to apply for jobs that use a computer program to make hiring decisions (Page 52)
- 22% of U.S. adults would be interested in applying for such jobs (Page 52)
- 37% of 18- to 29-year-olds are interested, compared to 21% of ages 30-49 and 16% of those 50 and older (Page 52)
- Men (27%) are more receptive than women (18%) (Page 52)
- College graduates (26%) are more receptive than those with some college (25%) or a high school diploma or less (17%) (Page 52)
- 76% of U.S. adults say they would not want to apply for jobs using a computer program for hiring (Page 53)
- 41% of respondents cite that computers can't capture everything about an applicant (Page 53)
- 20% of respondents are concerned the process would be too impersonal (Page 53)
- 22% of U.S. adults say they would want to apply (Page 53)
- Among those who would apply, 35% believe it would be more fair and less biased than humans (Page 53)
- Among those who would not apply, 41% believe computers can't capture everything about an applicant (Page 53)
- Survey conducted May 1-15, 2017 (Page 53)
- 66-year-old woman: "You have to talk to the applicant to see how they interact with HUMANS. This is ridiculous and scary..." (Page 54)
- 55-year-old woman: "Because it's idiotic. There are nuances to everything. Such a system denigrates the value of things a program cannot measure like work ethic, dedication, integrity, and commitment level." (Page 54)

pages.ocr_text: 5. Americans' attitudes toward hiring algorithms Robot caregivers are an example of a physical technology that replicates a tangible activity. But other examples of automation utilize large quantities of data and machine learning capabilities to automate elements of human thinking and decision-making, rather than physical tasks. The recommendation engines used by many e-commerce and streaming media platforms are a familiar example of this phenomenon. But these tools are increasingly being used by governments and commercial entities to make decisions with potentially profound consequences for ordinary Americans – such as whether or not they are able to receive a loan or are granted parole from prison. This survey examines Americans' attitudes towards these technologies using the scenario (highlighted in the accompanying sidebar) of an algorithm that makes hiring decisions using standardized information about job applicants. Despite the ubiquity of algorithms and machine learning in many aspects of life today, relatively few Americans have heard of or considered this specific scenario before. They express far more worry than enthusiasm about machines making these types of decisions, and few would personally want to apply for a job that used this type of computer program to hire job candidates. And although some feel that this type of program would be less biased and make better decisions than humans, a larger share expresses concern that many important qualities would be overlooked in the process. Scenario: Hiring algorithm Survey respondents were asked to read and respond to the following scenario: "Today, when companies are hiring they typically have someone read applicants' resumes and conduct personal interviews to choose the right person for the job. In the future, computer programs may be able to provide a systematic review of each applicant without the need for human involvement. These programs would give each applicant a score based on the content of their resumes, applications or standardized tests for skills such as problem solving or personality type. Applicants would then be ranked and hired based on those scores."

This page from the Pew Research Center presents findings on U.S. adults' attitudes toward hiring algorithms, comparing those who would and would not apply for jobs using such technology. The data, collected in a survey from May 1-15, 2017, shows that individuals interested in applying for these jobs have significantly more positive views. For example, 86% of this group find the concept realistic, compared to 52% of those not interested. Similarly, 52% of interested applicants expect the algorithm to do better than humans at hiring well-qualified candidates, versus only 17% of the non-interest group. The chart also reveals a stark contrast in worry levels, with 77% of interested applicants expressing some level of concern, compared to 35% of the non-interest group.

pages.ocr_text: Methodology The American Trends Panel (ATP), created by Pew Research Center, is a nationally representative panel of randomly selected U.S. adults recruited from landline and cellphone random-digit-dial surveys. Panelists participate via monthly self-administered web surveys. Panelists who do not have internet access are provided with a tablet and wireless internet connection. The panel is being managed by Abt Associates. Data in this report are drawn from the panel wave conducted May 1-May 15, 2017, among 4,135 respondents. The margin of sampling error for the full sample of 4,135 respondents is plus or minus 2.6 percentage points. Members of the American Trends Panel were recruited from two large, national landline and cellphone random-digit-dial (RDD) surveys conducted in English and Spanish. At the end of each survey, respondents were invited to join the panel. The first group of panelists was recruited from the 2014 Political Polarization and Typology Survey, conducted Jan.23-March 16, 2014. Of the 10,013 adults interviewed, 9,809 were invited to take part in the panel and a total of 5,338 agreed to participate. $^{1}$  The second group of panelists was recruited from the 2015 Survey on Government, conducted Aug. 27- Oct. 4, 2015. Of the 6,004 adults interviewed, all were invited to join the panel, and 2,976 agreed to participate. $^{2}$ The ATP data were weighted in a multistep process that begins with a base weight incorporating the respondents' original survey selection probability and the fact that in 2014 some panelists were subsampled for invitation to the panel. Next, an adjustment was made for the fact that the propensity to join the panel and remain an active panelist varied across different groups in the sample. The final step in the weighting uses an iterative technique that aligns the sample to population benchmarks on a number of dimensions. Gender, age, education, race, Hispanic origin and region parameters come from the U.S. Census Bureau's 2015 American Community Survey. The county-level population density parameter (deciles) comes from the 2010 U.S. Decennial Census. elements.text: Methodology

The American Trends Panel (ATP), created by Pew Research Center, is a nationally representative panel of randomly selected U.S. adults recruited from landline and cellphone random-digit-dial surveys. Panelists participate via monthly self-administered web surveys. Panelists who do not have internet access are provided with a tablet and wireless internet connection. The panel is being managed by Abt Associates.

Data in this report are drawn from the panel wave conducted May 1-May 15, 2017, among 4,135 respondents. The margin of sampling error for the full sample of 4,135 respondents is plus or minus 2.6 percentage points.

Members of the American Trends Panel were recruited from two large, national landline and cellphone random-digit-dial (RDD) surveys conducted in English and Spanish. At the end of each survey, respondents were invited to join the panel. The first group of panelists was recruited from the 2014 Political Polarization and Typology Survey, conducted Jan.23-March 16, 2014. Of the 10,013 adults interviewed, 9,809 were invited to take part in the panel and a total of 5,338 agreed to participate. $^{1}$  The second group of panelists was recruited from the 2015 Survey on Government, conducted Aug. 27- Oct. 4, 2015. Of the 6,004 adults interviewed, all were invited to join the panel, and 2,976 agreed to participate. $^{2}$

The ATP data were weighted in a multistep process that begins with a base weight incorporating the respondents' original survey selection probability and the fact that in 2014 some panelists were subsampled for invitation to the panel. Next, an adjustment was made for the fact that the propensity to join the panel and remain an active panelist varied across different groups in the sample. The final step in the weighting uses an iterative technique that aligns the sample to population benchmarks on a number of dimensions. Gender, age, education, race, Hispanic origin and region parameters come from the U.S. Census Bureau's 2015 American Community Survey. The county-level population density parameter (deciles) comes from the 2010 U.S. Decennial Census. The telephone service benchmark is comes from the January-June 2016 National Health Interview Survey and is projected to 2017. The volunteerism benchmark comes from the 2015 Current Population Survey Volunteer Supplement. The party affiliation benchmark is the average of the three most recent Pew Research Center general public telephone surveys. The Internet
